value: no prevailing magnetic direction of burrow axes (null)
method: field: species-level (second-order) axial direction of long straight tunnel segments of excavated burrow systems; magnetoreception inferred from burrow direction, not tested

value: avoided a blue (483 nm) light more than a red (631 nm) light, a 49% increase in the probability of avoidance (X21 = 6.35, P = 0.012)
method: behavioural: single-choice avoidance of a lit versus an unlit side of an arena, blue versus red LED
conditions: single-choice test in an outdoor arena: each goose chose between a side lit by one LED and an unlit side (choosing the lit side counted as attraction, the opposite side as avoidance); blue LED 483 nm at 80 cd (16,159 photons/cm2) and red LED 631 nm at 120 cd (18,056 photons/cm2), so the two lights were not equal in candela and the authors call their peak output radiometrically similar (Table S1); 23 wild Canada geese were collected in Marion County, Indiana, and 19 of 23 completed all eight treatments (blue or red, steady or 2 Hz pulsing, each on both sides); ambient light was not controlled, it was measured at the end of each trial and entered as a covariate (PCA1). The colour effect depended on trial order (colour by trial-order interaction X27 = 29.07, P = 0.00014): the Abstract says geese tended to avoid the blue light and move towards the red light, that they avoided red at the start and became attracted to it after further exposure, and the authors link this to a mere exposure effect, so the blue-over-red result is an average over an exposure sequence with no counterbalanced single-exposure control reported in the passages read. Birds were wild geese designated for euthanasia under a state management programme.

value: avoidance probability with a 2 Hz pulsing light (0.24) versus a steady light (0.19), difference not significant (P = 0.522)
method: behavioural: single-choice avoidance of a lit versus an unlit side of an arena, pulsing versus steady LED (colours pooled)
conditions: single-choice test in an outdoor arena: each goose chose between a side lit by one LED and an unlit side (choosing the lit side counted as attraction, the opposite side as avoidance); blue LED 483 nm at 80 cd (16,159 photons/cm2) and red LED 631 nm at 120 cd (18,056 photons/cm2), so the two lights were not equal in candela and the authors call their peak output radiometrically similar (Table S1); 23 wild Canada geese were collected in Marion County, Indiana, and 19 of 23 completed all eight treatments (blue or red, steady or 2 Hz pulsing, each on both sides); ambient light was not controlled, it was measured at the end of each trial and entered as a covariate (PCA1). This is the main effect of pulsing, tested across blue and red lights; the Abstract reports that pulsing at 2 Hz enhanced avoidance under high ambient light conditions and steady light enhanced avoidance under dim ambient light conditions (a pulsing by ambient light interaction), so the null main effect does not mean pulsing never mattered. Only one pulse rate (2 Hz) was tested, so no flicker threshold follows.

value: avoided the side lit by the 470-nm LED (16/17 birds, P = 0.000137) and the 630-nm LED (13/17 birds, P = 0.0245)
method: behavioural: single-choice avoidance of a lit versus an unlit side, five LED panels
conditions: wild-caught adult brown-headed cowbirds (33 in total, 30 males and three females) in outdoor aviaries, each bird tested on one LED type only (20 trials with 20 different cowbirds for each of five LED panels: 380 nm, 470 nm, 525 nm, 630 nm and cool white); single-choice test in which birds flew through an arena and chose a left or right exit, one side lit and the other unlit, in daylight; the reported denominators (16 or 17 birds per panel) are below 20 because trials with no choice were not analysed, and the paper gives no count of excluded birds. The LED panels were paired with resistors to maximize the brightness (and therefore contrast) of each panel and were not equated in radiance; the UV panel was the brightest, so brightness and contrast are confounded with wavelength; no table of LED radiance was found. A light-off control (18 birds, pooled across two phases) showed no left or right bias.

method: behavioural: single-choice avoidance of a lit versus an unlit side, five LED panels
conditions: wild-caught adult brown-headed cowbirds (33 in total, 30 males and three females) in outdoor aviaries, each bird tested on one LED type only (20 trials with 20 different cowbirds for each of five LED panels: 380 nm, 470 nm, 525 nm, 630 nm and cool white); single-choice test in which birds flew through an arena and chose a left or right exit, one side lit and the other unlit, in daylight; the reported denominators (16 or 17 birds per panel) are below 20 because trials with no choice were not analysed, and the paper gives no count of excluded birds. The 380-nm (UV) panel was the brightest, so the null for UV is not explained by a dim stimulus; the test has about 16 to 17 birds per panel, which limits power to detect a weak response.

value: naive butterflies visited red artificial flowers more often than expected among four colours (white, yellow, pink, red) (G = 29.19, df = 3, p = 0.0006)
method: behavioural: innate colour choice among four coloured artificial flowers
conditions: lab-reared adults 1 to 2 days old, from eggs laid by wild females near Tlaxcala, Mexico; Experiment 1: 32 butterflies, white, yellow, pink and red artificial flowers offered together (quadruple choice) after a 5-minute priming feed on black artificial flowers, then 30 minutes of free choice, under halogen lamps that emit no ultraviolet; the authors state they cannot rule out effects of the training on black targets on the later colour choice and suggest the red preference could be a more direct associative mechanism because red is close to black in overall intensity; reflectance of the plastic flowers was taken from an earlier study (Ornelas & Lara 2015), not measured in this paper; per-colour counts are not given in the passages read.
